cards.question: 매킨타이어 X는 공동체에서 빚·유산·기대·의무를 물려받는다고 했다. X가 본 정의의 출발점은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 물려받은 기대·의무 이행. 매킨타이어는 공동체로부터 물려받은 기대와 의무를 다하는 것이 정의의 출발점이라고 말했다.
criteria: 근거: 매킨타이어는 공동체로부터 물려받은 기대와 의무를 다하는 것이 정의의 출발점이라고 말했다.

cards.question: 삶의 영역별로 고유하고 특수한 다원적 분배 원칙을 적용해야 한다는 왈처의 개념은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 복합 평등. 왈처의 복합 평등은 삶의 영역별로 고유하고 특수한 다원적 분배 원칙을 적용해야 한다는 주장이다.
criteria: 근거: 왈처의 복합 평등은 삶의 영역별로 고유하고 특수한 다원적 분배 원칙을 적용해야 한다는 주장이다.

cards.question: 샌델이 말한 연고적 자아 X. X가 정체성을 형성하는 바탕은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 공동선 숙고와 연대 의식. 샌델은 인간이 공동선에 관한 숙고와 연대 의식을 바탕으로 공동체 구성원으로서 정체성을 형성한다고 보았고, 이를 연고적 자아라고 했다.
criteria: 근거: 샌델은 인간이 공동선에 관한 숙고와 연대 의식을 바탕으로 공동체 구성원으로서 정체성을 형성한다고 보았고, 이를 연고적 자아라고 했다.

cards.question: 법과 정치가 도덕 논쟁에 휘말리면 안 된다는 주장에 맞서 도덕적 중립은 불가능하다 한 사상가는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 샌델. 샌델은 도덕적 중립을 지키는 것은 처음부터 불가능하며, 좋은 삶이 무엇인지 함께 고민해야 한다고 말했다.
criteria: 근거: 샌델은 도덕적 중립을 지키는 것은 처음부터 불가능하며, 좋은 삶이 무엇인지 함께 고민해야 한다고 말했다.

cards.question: 과거 세대의 잘못에 대한 현세대의 책임 거부를 자유주의적 정의관은 어떻게 보나? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 정의에 어긋나지 않는다. 자유주의는 개인을 공동체의 역사로부터 독립된 존재로 보므로, 앞선 세대의 잘못을 현세대가 책임지지 않는 것을 부정의로 보지 않는다.
criteria: 근거: 자유주의는 개인을 공동체의 역사로부터 독립된 존재로 보므로, 앞선 세대의 잘못을 현세대가 책임지지 않는 것을 부정의로 보지 않는다.

cards.question: 투표 불참자에게 과태료 등을 부과하는 제도 X. 자유주의가 X에 반대하는 근거는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 불참으로 의견 낼 자유 제한. 자유주의는 투표에 참여하지 않는 것으로도 자신의 정치적 의견을 드러낼 수 있는데, 의무 투표제가 이런 개인의 자유를 제한한다며 반대한다.
criteria: 결론: 불참으로 의견 낼 자유 제한
근거: 자유주의는 투표에 참여하지 않는 것으로도 자신의 정치적 의견을 드러낼 수 있는데, 의무 투표제가 이런 개인의 자유를 제한한다며 반대한다.

cards.question: 초과 이윤세를 도입해 공익을 증진할 수 있다면 정의롭다고 평가하는 정의관은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 공동체주의적 정의관. 공동체주의적 정의관은 공동선(공익)의 실현을 정의로 보므로, 초과 이윤세로 공익을 증진할 수 있다면 정의롭다고 평가한다.
criteria: 근거: 공동체주의적 정의관은 공동선(공익)의 실현을 정의로 보므로, 초과 이윤세로 공익을 증진할 수 있다면 정의롭다고 평가한다.

cards.question: 총기 구매자 신원 조회를 강화하고 위험인물의 총기 소지를 막는 법 X. 공동체주의가 X에 찬성할 근거는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 공동체의 안전 보호. 공동체주의는 공동선(공익)의 실현을 정의로 보므로, 마스크 의무화처럼 공동체의 안전을 지킬 수 있다는 점에서 총기 규제에 찬성할 수 있다.
criteria: 근거: 공동체주의는 공동선(공익)의 실현을 정의로 보므로, 마스크 의무화처럼 공동체의 안전을 지킬 수 있다는 점에서 총기 규제에 찬성할 수 있다.

cards.question: 나이에 따라 영상물 시청을 제한하는 영상물 등급 제도 X. 자유주의가 X를 비판할 근거는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 개인의 선택권 제한. 자유주의는 국가가 특정 가치관을 강제할 수 없고 개인의 선택권과 자율성을 최대한 보장해야 한다고 보므로, 시청 제한을 선택권 제한으로 볼 수 있다.
criteria: 근거: 자유주의는 국가가 특정 가치관을 강제할 수 없고 개인의 선택권과 자율성을 최대한 보장해야 한다고 보므로, 시청 제한을 선택권 제한으로 볼 수 있다.

cards.question: 공동 목초지에 앞다투어 양을 방목한 마을의 목초지가 황폐해진 직접적 까닭은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 양이 풀을 더 빨리 뜯어 먹음. 공유지의 비극에서는 풀이 자라는 속도보다 양이 뜯어 먹는 속도가 빨라져 목초지가 빠르게 황폐해졌다.
criteria: 결론: 양이 풀을 더 빨리 뜯어 먹음
근거: 공유지의 비극에서는 풀이 자라는 속도보다 양이 뜯어 먹는 속도가 빨라져 목초지가 빠르게 황폐해졌다.

cards.question: 권리와 의무, 공익과 사익이 서로 영향을 끼친다는 관점 X. X에 따르면 사익만 추구할 경우는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 결국 사익도 추구 어려움. 권리와 의무, 공익과 사익은 서로 영향을 끼치므로 사익만을 추구하고 공익을 고려하지 않으면 결과적으로 사익도 추구하기 어려워진다.
criteria: 근거: 권리와 의무, 공익과 사익은 서로 영향을 끼치므로 사익만을 추구하고 공익을 고려하지 않으면 결과적으로 사익도 추구하기 어려워진다.

cards.question: 자유주의와 공동체주의 두 정의관의 관계 X는 상호 보완적이다. X로 볼 수 있는 까닭은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 개인 행복과 정의 사회 지향. 두 정의관은 궁극적으로 개인의 행복 추구와 정의로운 사회를 함께 지향한다는 점에서 상호 보완적 관계에 있다.
criteria: 결론: 개인 행복과 정의 사회 지향
근거: 두 정의관은 궁극적으로 개인의 행복 추구와 정의로운 사회를 함께 지향한다는 점에서 상호 보완적 관계에 있다.

cards.question: 사회 불평등에서 차등 분배되는 부·권력·명예 X. X를 달리 부르는 말은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 사회적 희소가치. 부·권력·명예 같은 사회적 자원은 누구나 원하지만 한정되어 있어 사회적 희소가치라고 부른다.
criteria: 근거: 부·권력·명예 같은 사회적 자원은 누구나 원하지만 한정되어 있어 사회적 희소가치라고 부른다.

cards.question: 양극화로 부모의 계층이 자녀에게 대물림될 때 형성되는 사회 구조는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 폐쇄적 사회 구조. 부모의 계층이 자녀에게 대물림되면 능력·업적에 따른 계층 이동이 어려운 폐쇄적 사회 구조가 형성된다.
criteria: 근거: 부모의 계층이 자녀에게 대물림되면 능력·업적에 따른 계층 이동이 어려운 폐쇄적 사회 구조가 형성된다.

cards.question: 계층을 상층·중층·하층으로 범주화해 수직적 연속선에 배열하는 이론 X. X를 제시한 학자는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 베버. 계층을 수직적 연속선상에 배열하고 다양한 요인으로 위치를 구분하는 계층 이론은 베버가 제시했다.
criteria: 근거: 계층을 수직적 연속선상에 배열하고 다양한 요인으로 위치를 구분하는 계층 이론은 베버가 제시했다.

cards.question: 지배 집단에 유리한 분배 구조가 계급을 재생산한다고 보는 이론 X. X에서 불평등을 결정하는 것은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 경제적 요인. 마르크스의 계급 이론은 경제적 요인이 다른 모든 사회 불평등을 결정한다고 보는 일원론이다.
criteria: 근거: 마르크스의 계급 이론은 경제적 요인이 다른 모든 사회 불평등을 결정한다고 보는 일원론이다.

cards.question: 권력은 크지만 재산은 적은 사람처럼 영역마다 계층 서열이 다른 현상은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 지위 불일치. 지위 불일치는 계급(재산), 위신(명예), 권력의 각 측면에서 개인의 서열 위치가 서로 다른 현상이다.
criteria: 근거: 지위 불일치는 계급(재산), 위신(명예), 권력의 각 측면에서 개인의 서열 위치가 서로 다른 현상이다.

cards.question: 계급·위신·권력의 서열이 서로 다른 현상 X. 마르크스 이론이 X를 설명하지 못하는 이유는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 경제적 요인만 보기 때문. 지위 불일치는 여러 요인을 함께 보는 계층 이론(다원론)만 설명할 수 있다. 경제적 요인 하나로만 보는 계급 이론은 설명하기 어렵다.
criteria: 근거: 지위 불일치는 여러 요인을 함께 보는 계층 이론(다원론)만 설명할 수 있다. 경제적 요인 하나로만 보는 계급 이론은 설명하기 어렵다.

cards.question: 이분법적·대립적 계급 구분이 타당했다고 평가받는 시기는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 근대 초 산업화 시기. 계급 구분은 근대 초 산업화 시기에는 타당했으나, 직업이 분화되고 복잡해진 현대 사회를 설명하기엔 적합하지 않다는 비판을 받는다.
criteria: 근거: 계급 구분은 근대 초 산업화 시기에는 타당했으나, 직업이 분화되고 복잡해진 현대 사회를 설명하기엔 적합하지 않다는 비판을 받는다.

cards.question: 신도심과 구도심 사이에 자원이 불균등하게 분배되어 생긴 격차 X. X의 종류는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 공간 불평등. 공간 불평등은 지역 간 자원이 불균등하게 분배되어 격차가 생기는 현상으로, 신도심과 구도심 같은 도시 내부에서도 나타난다.
criteria: 근거: 공간 불평등은 지역 간 자원이 불균등하게 분배되어 격차가 생기는 현상으로, 신도심과 구도심 같은 도시 내부에서도 나타난다.

cards.question: '성장 거점을 집중 개발해야 공간 불평등이 해소된다'는 주장이 틀린 이유는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 집중 개발이 격차를 낳음. 성장 가능성이 큰 지역에 자본과 기술을 집중 투자한 성장 거점 개발 정책은 제외된 지역의 인구 유출과 경제 침체를 낳아 공간 불평등의 원인이 되었다.
criteria: 근거: 성장 가능성이 큰 지역에 자본과 기술을 집중 투자한 성장 거점 개발 정책은 제외된 지역의 인구 유출과 경제 침체를 낳아 공간 불평등의 원인이 되었다.

cards.question: 교육·문화·의료 등 생활 환경의 지역 격차가 낙후 지역 주민에게 미치는 영향은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 삶의 질 저하. 공간 불평등으로 교육, 문화, 의료 등 생활 환경 전반이 불평등해지면 낙후 지역 주민의 삶의 질이 떨어진다.
criteria: 근거: 공간 불평등으로 교육, 문화, 의료 등 생활 환경 전반이 불평등해지면 낙후 지역 주민의 삶의 질이 떨어진다.

cards.question: 장애·나이·국적 등으로 소외되어 인간다운 삶을 영위하기 어려운 개인·집단은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 사회적 약자. 사회적 약자는 장애, 나이, 성별, 출신 국가, 소득 수준 등으로 사회적으로 소외되어 인간다운 삶을 영위하는 데 어려움을 겪는 개인이나 집단이다.
criteria: 근거: 사회적 약자는 장애, 나이, 성별, 출신 국가, 소득 수준 등으로 사회적으로 소외되어 인간다운 삶을 영위하는 데 어려움을 겪는 개인이나 집단이다.

cards.question: 신체적·문화적 특징으로 주류 집단에게 차별받는 사람들 X. X인지 판단하는 핵심은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 차별받는다는 사실. 사회적 소수자는 반드시 수적으로 소수를 뜻하지 않는다. 과거 남아프리카 공화국의 흑인처럼 다수여도 주류 집단에게 차별받으면 소수자다.
criteria: 근거: 사회적 소수자는 반드시 수적으로 소수를 뜻하지 않는다. 과거 남아프리카 공화국의 흑인처럼 다수여도 주류 집단에게 차별받으면 소수자다.

cards.question: 더 중요한 위치에 능력 있는 사람을 충원하려면 불평등이 불가피하다는 관점 X. X의 분배 기준은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 직업의 사회적 중요도. 기능론은 사회 전체의 필요에 의해 결정되는 직업별 사회적 중요도·기여도에 따라 차등 분배된다고 본다.
criteria: 근거: 기능론은 사회 전체의 필요에 의해 결정되는 직업별 사회적 중요도·기여도에 따라 차등 분배된다고 본다.

cards.question: 직업의 기능적 중요도에는 차이가 없다고 보는 관점 X. X가 본 불평등의 원인은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 지배 집단의 기득권 유지. 갈등론은 불평등을 지배 집단이 현재의 기득권과 지배적 위치를 유지하려는 결과로 본다.
criteria: 근거: 갈등론은 불평등을 지배 집단이 현재의 기득권과 지배적 위치를 유지하려는 결과로 본다.

cards.question: '의사의 소득이 높은 건 사회에 중요한 일을 맡아서다'라는 주장의 관점은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 기능론. 직업의 사회적 중요도·기여도에 따라 보상이 차등 분배된다고 보는 것은 기능론의 관점이다.
criteria: 근거: 직업의 사회적 중요도·기여도에 따라 보상이 차등 분배된다고 보는 것은 기능론의 관점이다.

cards.question: 좋은 직업이 부모의 재산과 배경으로 대물림된다고 보는 관점 X. X가 받는 비판은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 개인 노력의 영향 간과. 갈등론은 개인의 능력이나 노력이 지위 변동에 미치는 영향력을 간과한다는 비판을 받는다.
criteria: 근거: 갈등론은 개인의 능력이나 노력이 지위 변동에 미치는 영향력을 간과한다는 비판을 받는다.

cards.question: 불평등이 사회적 박탈감과 집단 간 대립을 유발한다는 관점 X. X가 본 가치 배분의 성격은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 강제적·불공정. 갈등론은 가치가 지배 집단만의 합의에 의해 강제적으로 불공정하게 배분된다고 본다.
criteria: 근거: 갈등론은 가치가 지배 집단만의 합의에 의해 강제적으로 불공정하게 배분된다고 본다.

cards.question: 불평등을 개인을 적재적소에 배치하는 장치로 보는 관점 X. X가 경시한다고 비판받는 것은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 소외된 사람들의 현실. 기능론은 가정 배경 같은 현실적 영향력을 간과하고, 불평등이 초래하는 대립·갈등과 소외된 사람들의 현실을 경시한다는 비판을 받는다.
criteria: 근거: 기능론은 가정 배경 같은 현실적 영향력을 간과하고, 불평등이 초래하는 대립·갈등과 소외된 사람들의 현실을 경시한다는 비판을 받는다.

cards.question: 조세로 국가·지자체가 전액 지원해 최저 생활을 보장하는 제도 X. X의 복지 이념은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 선별적 복지. 공공 부조는 생활이 어려운 저소득층(절대 빈곤층)을 골라 지원하는 선별적 복지다.
criteria: 근거: 공공 부조는 생활이 어려운 저소득층(절대 빈곤층)을 골라 지원하는 선별적 복지다.

cards.question: 가입자·사업주가 보험료를 내고 국가가 일부 보태는 제도 X. X의 한계는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 보험료 부담. 사회 보험의 한계는 보험료 부담이다. 부정적 낙인과 국가 재정 부담은 공공 부조의 한계다.
criteria: 근거: 사회 보험의 한계는 보험료 부담이다. 부정적 낙인과 국가 재정 부담은 공공 부조의 한계다.

cards.question: 사회 보험료를 소득 수준에 따라 다르게 내는 것은 어떤 원칙인가? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 능력별 부담. 사회 보험의 재원은 수익자 부담과 능력별 부담 원칙을 따르며, 소득에 따라 보험료를 달리 내는 것은 능력별 부담이다.
criteria: 근거: 사회 보험의 재원은 수익자 부담과 능력별 부담 원칙을 따르며, 소득에 따라 보험료를 달리 내는 것은 능력별 부담이다.

cards.question: 공공 부조가 사회 보험보다 소득 재분배 효과가 큰 까닭은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 부담자와 수혜자가 다름. 공공 부조는 조세로 마련한 재원을 저소득층에게 지원해 부담자와 수혜자가 달라 소득 재분배 효과가 크다.
criteria: 근거: 공공 부조는 조세로 마련한 재원을 저소득층에게 지원해 부담자와 수혜자가 달라 소득 재분배 효과가 크다.

cards.question: 1차 사회 안전망에서 빠진 빈곤층을 받치는 2차 안전망 X. X의 한계는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 수혜자 낙인 우려. 2차 안전망은 공공 부조다. 공공 부조는 수혜자 선정 과정에서 부정적 낙인이 생기고 국가 재정 부담이 크다는 한계가 있다.
criteria: 근거: 2차 안전망은 공공 부조다. 공공 부조는 수혜자 선정 과정에서 부정적 낙인이 생기고 국가 재정 부담이 크다는 한계가 있다.

cards.question: 농어촌 학생 전형·기회균등 전형이 속하는 제도 X. X가 받는 비판은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 개인 능력·노력 경시. 적극적 평등 실현 조치는 역차별 논란과 함께 개인의 능력·노력을 고려하지 않는다는 비판을 받는다.
criteria: 근거: 적극적 평등 실현 조치는 역차별 논란과 함께 개인의 능력·노력을 고려하지 않는다는 비판을 받는다.

cards.question: 여성 할당제로 남성이 불이익을 받는다는 논란 X. X를 줄이려면 시행 시 무엇이 필요한가? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 사회적 합의. 보호하려던 쪽 대신 반대쪽이 차별받는다는 역차별 논란이 생길 수 있으므로 시행할 때 사회적 합의가 필요하다.
criteria: 근거: 보호하려던 쪽 대신 반대쪽이 차별받는다는 역차별 논란이 생길 수 있으므로 시행할 때 사회적 합의가 필요하다.

cards.question: 장애인 의무 고용 제도에 대한 설명으로 옳은 것은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 민간 기업에도 적용. 장애인 의무 고용 제도는 국가·지자체뿐 아니라 일정 규모 이상의 공공 기관과 민간 기업에 장애인 고용을 의무화한 적극적 평등 실현 조치다.
criteria: 근거: 장애인 의무 고용 제도는 국가·지자체뿐 아니라 일정 규모 이상의 공공 기관과 민간 기업에 장애인 고용을 의무화한 적극적 평등 실현 조치다.

cards.question: 공공 기관 지방 이전과 혁신 도시 조성을 담은 법 X. X가 해결하려는 문제는? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 수도권 과밀화. 「국가 균형 발전 특별법」에 따른 공공 기관 지방 이전과 혁신 도시 조성은 수도권 과밀화 해소 정책이다.
criteria: 근거: 「국가 균형 발전 특별법」에 따른 공공 기관 지방 이전과 혁신 도시 조성은 수도권 과밀화 해소 정책이다.

cards.question: 지역 격차 완화 정책이 궁극적으로 이루려는 것은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 국토의 균형 발전. 지역 격차 완화 정책은 공간 불평등을 해소하여 국토의 균형 발전을 이루려는 정책이다.
criteria: 근거: 지역 격차 완화 정책은 공간 불평등을 해소하여 국토의 균형 발전을 이루려는 정책이다.

cards.question: 청소년 참여 포털에 필요한 정책을 올리는 것은 어떤 시민 실천인가? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 정책 제안. 청소년 참여 포털에서 정책을 제안하는 것은 정의로운 사회를 위해 필요한 정책을 다양한 방식으로 제안하는 실천이다.
criteria: 근거: 청소년 참여 포털에서 정책을 제안하는 것은 정의로운 사회를 위해 필요한 정책을 다양한 방식으로 제안하는 실천이다.

cards.question: 국가의 최고법인 헌법은 인권을 국민의 X(으)로 명시해 보장한다. X는?
cards.explanation: 헌법은 국가의 최고법으로, 인권을 국민의 기본권으로 명시하여 헌법에 보장한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법이 추구하는 궁극의 가치이자 모든 기본권의 근거는?
cards.explanation: 인간으로서의 존엄과 가치는 헌법이 추구하는 궁극의 가치이며, 모든 기본권의 근거이자 국가 권력 행사의 기준이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 인간으로서의 존엄과 가치에 대한 설명으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 인간은 인간이라는 이유만으로 존중받아야 하므로, 다른 목적을 위한 수단으로 이용하거나 인격을 훼손해서는 안 된다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 모든 기본권의 근거 A, 국가의 간섭을 받지 않을 권리 B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 인간으로서의 존엄과 가치는 모든 기본권의 근거이고, 국가 권력의 간섭을 받지 않고 자유롭게 생활할 권리는 자유권이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국가 권력의 간섭을 받지 않고 자유롭게 생활할 수 있는 권리는?
cards.explanation: 자유권은 국가 권력의 간섭을 받지 않고 자유롭게 생활할 수 있는 권리로, 국가의 개입을 막는 방어적·소극적 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 자유권의 성격에 대한 설명으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 자유권은 헌법에 구체적으로 열거되지 않은 자유도 보장되는 포괄적 권리이며, 국가의 개입을 막는 소극적 권리다. 국가의 개입이 전제되는 것은 사회권·청구권이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 신체의 자유, 종교의 자유, 직업 선택의 자유가 속하는 기본권은?
cards.explanation: 신체의 자유, 종교의 자유, 언론·출판·집회·결사의 자유, 직업 선택의 자유 등은 자유권의 내용이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 성별·종교·사회적 신분으로 차별받지 않고 동등하게 대우받을 권리는?
cards.explanation: 평등권은 모든 국민이 성별, 종교, 사회적 신분 등에 의해 차별받지 않고 동등하게 대우받을 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 평등권에 대한 설명으로 옳은 것은?
cards.explanation: 평등권은 합당한 근거 없이 불평등한 대우를 받지 않을 권리다. 합리적인 근거가 있는 차등까지 모두 금지하는 것은 아니다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 투표권·피선거권·국민 투표권이 속하는 기본권 X. X의 의미는?
cards.explanation: 투표권, 피선거권, 국민 투표권은 참정권이다. 참정권은 국가의 의사 결정에 참여할 수 있는 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 참정권에 대한 설명으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 참정권은 국가의 의사 결정에 참여할 수 있는 권리로 투표권·피선거권·국민 투표권 등이 있으며, 원칙적으로 외국인에게는 인정되지 않는다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 19세기 영국 노동자들이 벌인 차티스트 운동과 관련 깊은 기본권은?
cards.explanation: 차티스트 운동은 노동자들이 선거권 확대를 요구한 운동으로, 국가의 의사 결정에 참여할 권리인 참정권과 관련 깊다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국민이 국가에 인간다운 생활의 보장을 요구할 수 있는 권리는?
cards.explanation: 사회권은 국민이 국가에 인간다운 생활의 보장을 적극적으로 요구할 수 있는 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 다른 기본권이 침해되었을 때 구제를 요구할 수 있는 수단적 권리는?
cards.explanation: 청구권은 다른 기본권이 침해되었을 때 이의 구제를 요구할 수 있는 권리로, 기본권을 지키기 위한 수단적 성격의 기본권이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국가의 개입이 전제되어야 보장되는 기본권 A, B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 사회권은 국가에 인간다운 생활 보장을, 청구권은 침해된 기본권의 구제를 요구하는 권리로 둘 다 국가의 개입이 전제되어야 보장된다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국가에 대한 소극적 권리 A, 국가에 적극적으로 요구하는 권리 B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 자유권은 국가의 간섭을 막는 소극적 권리이고, 사회권은 국가에 인간다운 생활의 보장을 적극적으로 요구하는 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 인간의 존엄과 인간 존중을 위한 본질적 권리로 묶이는 A, B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 자유권과 평등권은 인간의 존엄과 인간 존중을 위한 본질적 권리로 정리된다. 사회권·청구권은 국가의 개입이 전제되는 권리다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 제37조 ②가 기본권 제한의 목적으로 들지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 헌법 제37조 ②는 국가 안전 보장, 질서 유지 또는 공공복리를 위하여 필요한 경우에 한하여 기본권을 제한할 수 있다고 정한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 제37조 ②에 따르면 기본권은 무엇으로써 제한할 수 있는가?
cards.explanation: 국민의 모든 자유와 권리는 필요한 경우에 한하여 국회가 만든 법률로써 제한할 수 있다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 기본권을 법률로 제한하는 경우에도 침해할 수 없는 것은?
cards.explanation: 헌법 제37조 ②에 따라 기본권을 제한하는 경우에도 자유와 권리의 본질적인 내용을 침해할 수 없다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 기본권 제한의 한계에 대한 설명으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 기본권은 정당한 목적을 달성하는 데 필요한 범위 안에서만 제한해야 하며, 보호하려는 공익이 침해되는 개인의 이익보다 커야 한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 법률은 국회, 명령은 행정부가 만든다. 조례와 규칙을 만드는 기관을 차례로 알맞게 나열한 것은?
cards.explanation: 법률은 국회, 명령은 행정부가 만드는 중앙 차원의 법이고, 조례는 지방 의회, 규칙은 지방 자치 단체장(지방 행정부)이 만드는 지방 차원의 법이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국가 권력을 나누어 각 기관이 서로 견제와 균형을 이루게 하는 제도는?
cards.explanation: 권력 분립 제도는 국가 권력을 나누어 각각 다른 기관에 분담시켜 상호 견제와 균형을 이루도록 하는 제도다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 권력 분립 제도로 막으려는 것은?
cards.explanation: 권력 분립 제도는 각 국가 기관의 권력 남용을 막아 국민의 자유와 권리를 보장하기 위한 제도다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 우리나라 삼권 분립에서 입법권 A, 사법권 B가 속한 곳은? A–B는?
cards.explanation: 입법권은 국회, 행정권은 정부, 사법권은 법원에 속하는 삼권 분립 제도를 실시한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 입법권과 집행권의 2권 분립 A, 입법·행정·사법의 3권 분립 B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 로크는 입법권과 집행권(행정권이 사법권을 포함)의 2권 분립을, 몽테스키외는 입법권·집행권·사법권의 3권 분립을 주장했다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 로크의 2권 분립과 이어지는 정부 형태 A, 몽테스키외의 3권 분립과 이어지는 B는?
cards.explanation: 로크의 2권 분립은 입법부와 행정부가 융합된 의원 내각제로, 몽테스키외의 3권 분립은 권력이 서로 견제하는 대통령제로 이어진다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 일반적인 민사·형사 재판의 3심제에서 1심 A, 2심 B를 맡는 법원은? A–B는?
cards.explanation: 일반적인 민사·형사 재판에서 1심은 지방 법원, 2심은 고등 법원, 3심은 대법원이 맡는다. 가정 법원은 가사·소년 사건을 맡는 전문 법원이라 일반 재판의 1심이 아니다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 국민이 선거로 대표자를 뽑아 국민의 의사와 이익을 정치에 반영하는 제도는?
cards.explanation: 민주적 선거 제도는 국민이 선거를 통해 국가를 운영할 대표자를 선출하여 국민의 의사와 이익을 정치에 반영하도록 하는 제도다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 일정 나이의 모든 국민에게 주어지는 A와 공무 담임권. A는?
cards.explanation: 민주적 선거 제도의 내용으로 일정 나이의 모든 국민에게 선거권과 공무 담임권을 부여한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 선거의 공정성과 기회균등을 위해 국가가 선거를 관리하고 비용을 지원하는 제도는?
cards.explanation: 선거 공영제는 선거의 공정성과 기회균등을 보장하기 위해 국가가 선거 과정을 관리하고 비용을 지원하는 제도다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 선거구를 법률로 확정하게 하는 원칙 X. X가 막으려는 것은?
cards.explanation: 선거구 법정주의는 선거구를 법률로 확정하게 하여, 특정 정당이나 후보에게 유리하게 선거구를 나누는 게리맨더링을 막는다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 누구나 정당을 세울 수 있고 여러 정당이 자유롭게 활동하게 하는 제도는?
cards.explanation: 정당 설립의 자유와 복수 정당 제도는 국민의 다양한 정치적 견해가 정책 결정에 반영되게 하여 민주적 기본 질서를 유지한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 정당 설립의 자유와 복수 정당 제도의 내용으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 정당은 등록제로 운영되며 허가제가 아니다. 국가는 정당에 보조금을 지급한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 인권을 침해받은 국민이 국가 기관을 통해 권리를 구제받는 제도는?
cards.explanation: 기본권 구제 제도는 인권을 침해받은 국민이 사안에 따라 국가의 기본권 구제 기관을 통해 권리를 구제받을 수 있게 하는 제도다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 법원의 재판과 함께 기본권 구제 제도에 속하는 헌법재판소 심판 A, B는?
cards.explanation: 기본권 구제 제도에는 법원의 재판, 헌법재판소의 위헌 법률 심판과 헌법 소원 심판이 있다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 해석과 관련한 분쟁을 해결하며 헌법을 수호하는 기관은?
cards.explanation: 헌법재판소는 헌법 해석과 관련한 분쟁을 해결하는 기관으로, 헌법을 수호하고 국민의 기본권을 보장하는 역할을 한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 재판의 전제가 되는 법률의 위헌 여부를 가리는 심판 X. X를 제청하는 곳은?
cards.explanation: 위헌 법률 심판은 법원의 제청에 따라 재판의 전제가 되는 법률이 헌법에 위반되는지를 판단한다. 재판 당사자는 법원에 제청을 신청할 수 있다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 공권력에 의해 침해된 기본권을 구제하기 위한 헌법재판소의 심판은?
cards.explanation: 헌법 소원 심판은 헌법에 보장된 국민의 기본권이 공권력에 의하여 침해되었을 때 이를 구제하기 위한 심판이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 소원 심판에 대한 설명으로 옳지 않은 것은?
cards.explanation: 공권력으로 기본권을 침해당한 국민은 누구나 헌법 소원을 청구할 수 있지만 최후의 수단이다. 법원의 재판은 헌법 소원의 대상에서 제외된다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 재판 당사자의 위헌 법률 심판 제청 신청을 법원이 기각했다. 당사자가 할 수 있는 것은?
cards.explanation: 법원이 위헌 법률 심판 제청 신청을 기각하면, 재판 당사자는 헌법재판소에 위헌 심사형 헌법 소원을 청구할 수 있다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 공무원 시험의 응시 나이 제한으로 기본권을 침해당해 청구한 심판 유형은?
cards.explanation: 공권력 행사로 직접 기본권을 침해당해 청구하는 것은 권리 구제형 헌법 소원이다. 응시 나이 제한 사건이 그 예다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 위헌이지만 즉시 효력을 잃으면 혼란이 커서 법 개정 때까지 효력을 인정하는 결정은?
cards.explanation: 헌법 불합치 결정은 법률이 헌법에 맞지 않지만, 갑자기 효력을 잃으면 법적 혼란이 생기므로 관련 법이 개정될 때까지 한시적으로 효력을 인정하는 결정이다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 소원에서 청구 요건을 갖추지 못한 경우 A, 청구가 받아들여진 경우 B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 요건을 갖추지 못하면 각하, 청구 이유가 없으면(합헌) 기각, 청구가 받아들여지면(위헌) 인용 결정을 내린다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법재판소 재판관 9명을 정하는 방식으로 옳은 것은?
cards.explanation: 재판관 9명 중 3명은 국회가 선출하고 3명은 대법원장이 지명하며 3명은 대통령이 정한다. 헌법재판소장은 국회의 동의를 얻어 대통령이 임명한다.

cards.question: 기본권을 침해당했다며 헌법 소원 심판을 청구할 때, 그 대상이 될 수 없는 것은?
cards.explanation: 헌법 소원은 공권력으로 기본권을 침해당한 국민이 청구한다. 법률이나 시험 규정, 경찰의 공권력 행사도 대상이 될 수 있지만, 법원의 재판은 헌법 소원의 대상에서 제외된다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 인권 침해를 조사하고 구제하는 독립된 종합 인권 전담 기구는?
cards.explanation: 국가 인권 위원회는 독립된 종합 인권 전담 기구로, 인권 침해를 조사하고 구제 조치를 한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 고충 민원 처리와 불합리한 행정 제도 개선을 맡는 기관은?
cards.explanation: 국민 권익 위원회는 고충 민원을 처리하고 불합리한 행정 제도를 개선하며, 공무원 부패 신고 등을 받아 부패를 방지한다.
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 인권 침해 구제 기관 A, 공무원 부패 신고를 받는 기관 B. A–B는?
cards.explanation: 국가 인권 위원회는 인권 침해를 구제하고, 국민 권익 위원회는 공무원 부패 신고와 고충 민원을 처리한다.

cards.question: 자유권과 사회권·청구권의 차이를 국가의 역할을 중심으로 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 자유권은 국가 권력의 간섭을 받지 않고 자유롭게 생활할 권리로, 국가의 개입을 막는 소극적·방어적 권리다. 사회권은 국가에 인간다운 생활의 보장을 적극적으로 요구하는 권리이고, 청구권은 다른 기본권이 침해되었을 때 구제를 요구하는 수단적 권리다. 사회권과 청구권은 국가의 개입이 전제되어야 보장된다.
criteria: 사회권: 인간다운 생활 보장을 적극적으로 요구
cards.source_label: 조안나T 학습 노트 · 주제 3 인권 보장을 위한 헌법의 역할

cards.question: 헌법 제37조 ②에 나타난 기본권 제한의 목적·형식·한계를 서술하시오.
cards.answer: 국가 안전 보장, 질서 유지 또는 공공복리를 위하여 필요한 경우에 한하여 국회가 만든 법률로써 기본권을 제한할 수 있다. 제한하는 경우에도 자유와 권리의 본질적인 내용은 침해할 수 없으며, 정당한 목적을 달성하는 데 필요한 범위 안에서만, 보호하려는 공익이 침해되는 개인의 이익보다 클 때 제한해야 한다.
criteria: 필요한 범위 안에서, 공익이 사익보다 커야 함

cards.question: 권력 분립 제도의 의미와 목적을 쓰고, 로크와 몽테스키외의 권력 분립론을 정부 형태와 연결해 비교하시오.
cards.answer: 권력 분립 제도는 국가 권력을 나누어 각각 다른 기관에 분담시켜 상호 견제와 균형을 이루도록 하는 제도로, 각 국가 기관의 권력 남용을 막아 국민의 자유와 권리를 보장하기 위한 것이다. 로크는 입법권과 집행권의 2권 분립을 주장했고 이는 입법부와 행정부가 융합된 의원 내각제로 이어진다. 몽테스키외는 입법권·행정권·사법권의 3권 분립을 주장했고 이는 권력이 서로 견제하는 대통령제로 이어진다.
criteria: 목적: 권력 남용 방지 → 자유와 권리 보장

cards.question: 위헌 법률 심판과 헌법 소원 심판을 청구(제청) 주체와 목적을 중심으로 비교하시오.
cards.answer: 위헌 법률 심판은 재판의 전제가 되는 법률이 헌법에 위반되는지를 판단하는 심판으로, 법원이 헌법재판소에 제청한다. 재판 당사자는 법원에 제청을 신청할 수 있고, 법원이 이를 기각하면 위헌 심사형 헌법 소원을 청구할 수 있다. 헌법 소원 심판은 공권력에 의해 헌법상 기본권을 침해당한 국민이 직접 청구하여 구제받는 심판으로, 최후의 수단이며 법원의 재판은 대상에서 제외된다.
criteria: 위헌 법률 심판: 법원이 제청, 법률의 위헌 여부 판단
헌법 소원: 기본권을 침해당한 국민이 청구, 구제 목적
제청 신청 기각 시 위헌 심사형 헌법 소원
헌법 소원은 최후 수단, 법원 재판은 제외

cards.badge: Made of stone, the city still stands.
cards.question: 문장 앞에 생략된 접속사로 알맞은 것은?
cards.passage:
Chichén Itzá was a major city of the Maya Empire from A.D. 750 to 1200. Made of stepped pyramids, temples, and other stone structures, the ancient city is now one of Mexico’s most visited tourist destinations. The largest building in Chichén Itzá is the Temple of Kukulkan ―a pyramid with 365 steps. A kind of calendar, the temple shows the change of seasons. On the spring and autumn equinoxes each year, a shadow falls on the pyramid in the shape of a snake. As the sun sets, this shadowy snake goes down the steps to eventually join a carved snake head on the pyramid’s side. The Mayans constructed the pyramids with carved stone. Amazingly, they worked without wheels or metal tools. To build a pyramid, Mayan workers created a base and added smaller and smaller levels as the structure rose. Building the pyramids required many workers. Some pyramids took hundreds of years to complete. Chichén Itzá was both an advanced city center and a religious site. Spanish records show that the Mayans made human sacrifices to a rain god here. Archaeologists have found bones, jewelry, and other objects that people wore when they were sacrificed. Experts also know that the Mayans were knowledgeable astronomers. They used the tops of the pyramids to view Venus and other planets.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.explanation: Made of stone은 이유를 나타내는 분사구문이다. Because(As) it is made of stone에서 접속사·주어·be동사가 생략됐다.

Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Türkiye, is one of the oldest man-made structures on Earth. Experts believe it was built about 12,000 years ago. The structure consists of dozens of stone pillars arranged in rings. Many pillars are covered with carvings of animals. The tallest pillars are 5.5 meters in height and weigh more than 14,500 kilograms. At the time that Göbekli Tepe was built, there was no writing system, and people did not use metal. Even wheels did not exist. Amazingly, though, the builders were able to cut, shape, and transport 16-ton stones. Archaeologists found Stone Age tools such as knives at the site. They think hundreds of workers carved and put the pillars in place. Archaeologists are still debating the purpose of Göbekli Tepe. Klaus Schmidt ― the archaeologist who originally excavated the site ― believed that Göbekli Tepe was a holy meeting place. According to his theory, the T-shaped pillars represent human beings. The pillars face the center of the circle and perhaps represent a religious ceremony. New evidence suggests that large feasts took place at the site. Archaeologists found thousands of small animal bones nearby, with stone containers large enough to hold more than 150 liters of liquid. They also found smaller pillars similar to Göbekli Tepe’s in areas over 200 kilometers away. It’s as though Göbekli Tepe were a cathedral and the other structures were local churches.

cards.passage:
For hundreds of years, Machu Picchu remained hidden in the Andes Mountains of Peru. In 1911, an American explorer named Hiram Bingham introduced the ancient city to the world after local people guided him there. Today, millions of visitors travel to see its beautiful stone buildings and breathtaking mountain views. Although many facts about Machu Picchu are known, historians still debate why the city was built and why it was later abandoned. Most experts believe that Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s during the rule of the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The city was probably home to nobles, priests, and skilled workers rather than a large population. People grew crops on stone terraces that covered the mountainside. They also collected fresh water through a system of carefully planned canals and fountains. These features allowed people to live comfortably in a place that was difficult to reach. One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

In 1911, an American explorer named Hiram Bingham introduced the ancient city to the world after local people guided him there. Although many facts about Machu Picchu are known, historians still debate why the city was built and why it was later abandoned. Most experts believe that Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s during the rule of the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The city was probably home to nobles, priests, and skilled workers rather than a large population. People grew crops on stone terraces that covered the mountainside. They also collected fresh water through a system of carefully planned canals and fountains. These features allowed people to live comfortably in a place that was difficult to reach. One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

cards.badge: a person who copied legal documents by hand
cards.question: 이런 일을 한 사람을 뜻하는 말은?
cards.passage:
I am an elderly man. For the past thirty years, my work as a lawyer has brought me into contact with a particular class of men: the law-copyists, or scriveners. I have known many of them, and could tell many stories that might make you smile or weep. But I’ll leave out the biographies of all other scriveners for a few passages from the life of Bartleby, who was the strangest I ever saw or heard of. At the time of this story, my office was located on Wall Street. On one side, my windows looked out upon the white wall of the interior of a spacious sky-light shaft. On the other side, my windows commanded an unobstructed view of a lofty brick wall, black by age and everlasting shade. This view was not exactly beautiful, but it was at least quiet. I already had two scriveners: Turkey and Nippers. Turkey was a short, fat Englishman who worked wonderfully in the morning, but after his lunch, his face would turn red, and he became energetic but reckless and messy with his ink. Nippers, on the other hand, was a victim of ambition and indigestion. He was nervous and irritable in the morning, but calm and productive in the afternoon. Between them, I had a functional office, provided it was the right time of day. There was also Ginger Nut, my twelve-year-old errand boy, whose most important duty was to buy apples and ginger nuts for the scriveners. But as my business grew, I needed more help. In answer to my advertisement, a young man appeared on my office threshold one morning. He was pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, and incurably forlorn. He was Bartleby. After a brief interview, I hired him. I gave him a seat at a desk near my own, separated by a high green screen. I wanted him to be close enough for me to hand him papers, but private enough to keep his quiet nature intact.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.explanation: scrivener(필경사)는 법률 문서와 계약서를 손으로 베껴 쓰던 사람이다. 기계 부품처럼 대체 가능한 존재로 취급됐다.

I am an elderly man. For the past thirty years, my work as a lawyer has brought me into contact with a particular class of men: the law-copyists, or scriveners. I have known many of them, and could tell many stories that might make you smile or weep. But I’ll leave out the biographies of all other scriveners for a few passages from the life of Bartleby, who was the strangest I ever saw or heard of. At the time of this story, my office was located on Wall Street. On one side, my windows looked out upon the white wall of the interior of a spacious sky-light shaft. On the other side, my windows commanded an unobstructed view of a lofty brick wall, black by age and everlasting shade. This view was not exactly beautiful, but it was at least quiet. I already had two scriveners: Turkey and Nippers. Turkey was a short, fat Englishman who worked wonderfully in the morning, but after his lunch, his face would turn red, and he became energetic but reckless and messy with his ink. Nippers, on the other hand, was a victim of ambition and indigestion. He was nervous and irritable in the morning, but calm and productive in the afternoon. Between them, I had a functional office, provided it was the right time of day. There was also Ginger Nut, my twelve-year-old errand boy, whose most important duty was to buy apples and ginger nuts for the scriveners. But as my business grew, I needed more help. In answer to my advertisement, a young man appeared on my office threshold one morning. He was pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, and incurably forlorn. He was Bartleby. After a brief interview, I hired him. I gave him a seat at a desk near my own, separated by a high green screen. I wanted him to be close enough for me to hand him papers, but private enough to keep his quiet nature intact.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
Nippers was a victim of ambition and indigestion.
cards.explanation: a victim of A = A에 시달리는 사람. 야망이 지나쳐 불만이 많고 소화불량도 있었다.

cards.question: isolation의 뜻은?
cards.passage:
I am an elderly man. For the past thirty years, my work as a lawyer has brought me into contact with a particular class of men: the law-copyists, or scriveners. I have known many of them, and could tell many stories that might make you smile or weep. But I’ll leave out the biographies of all other scriveners for a few passages from the life of Bartleby, who was the strangest I ever saw or heard of. At the time of this story, my office was located on Wall Street. On one side, my windows looked out upon the white wall of the interior of a spacious sky-light shaft. On the other side, my windows commanded an unobstructed view of a lofty brick wall, black by age and everlasting shade. This view was not exactly beautiful, but it was at least quiet. I already had two scriveners: Turkey and Nippers. Turkey was a short, fat Englishman who worked wonderfully in the morning, but after his lunch, his face would turn red, and he became energetic but reckless and messy with his ink. Nippers, on the other hand, was a victim of ambition and indigestion. He was nervous and irritable in the morning, but calm and productive in the afternoon. Between them, I had a functional office, provided it was the right time of day. There was also Ginger Nut, my twelve-year-old errand boy, whose most important duty was to buy apples and ginger nuts for the scriveners. But as my business grew, I needed more help. In answer to my advertisement, a young man appeared on my office threshold one morning. He was pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, and incurably forlorn. He was Bartleby. After a brief interview, I hired him. I gave him a seat at a desk near my own, separated by a high green screen. I wanted him to be close enough for me to hand him papers, but private enough to keep his quiet nature intact.

cards.explanation: isolation은 "고립, 소외"다. 건물 숲 한가운데서 느끼는 심리적 고립이다.

cards.badge: He copied by sunlight and by candlelight.
cards.question: 이 표현이 뜻하는 것은?
cards.passage:
At first, Bartleby did an extraordinary amount of writing. As if long famishing for something to copy, he eagerly copied my documents. He copied by sunlight and by candlelight. I would have been pleased with his hard work if he had worked cheerfully. But he wrote on silently, palely, mechanically. It was on the third day of his employment that the first crack appeared in this routine. I had a document that needed to be compared for accuracy. I called to Bartleby, asking him to step behind the screen to help me check a few lines. Without moving from his seat, Bartleby replied in a unusually gentle and firm voice: “I would prefer not to.” I sat in stunned silence. I thought my ears had deceived me. I repeated my request, but the response was exactly the same. “I would prefer not to.” I looked at him. He was perfectly calm. There was no sign of anger, impatience, or rudeness in his face. Had he seemed angry or rude, I would have fired him immediately. But his calmness fascinated and paralyzed me. I could not make myself argue with him. As days passed, the situation grew more bizarre. One morning, I asked him to go to the post office; he replied that he would prefer not to. I asked him to call the other clerks to help with a task; he preferred not to. Eventually, I discovered that he had stopped writing altogether. He would spend hours standing behind his screen, staring out the window at the dead brick wall. I tried to talk to him and persuade him. “Bartleby,” I said, “why will you not write? Why will you not do anything?” “I would prefer not to,” he replied, and nothing more.

My emotions toward him were a strange mixture. Sometimes I felt a deep, melancholy pity. I realized that Bartleby was alone in the world — a lonely soul in the middle of the busy, commercial desert of Wall Street. I discovered that he never ate a full dinner; he lived almost entirely on ginger nuts. Even more shockingly, I found out one Sunday morning that he was actually living in the office. He slept on the sofa, washed his face in a small basin, and spent his weekends in the total silence of the empty business district. However, pity soon turned to a sense of dread. His presence began to affect the atmosphere of the office. I found myself, and even Turkey and Nippers, unconsciously using the word ‘prefer’ in our daily speech. His passive resistance was like a quiet plague. I felt that my authority was slowly fading before a man who did nothing, said nothing, and wanted nothing. When I finally told him he must leave, he simply preferred not to. I offered him money; he let it lie on the table. I realized that as long as he remained in my office, he was my responsibility. But the pressure from my professional friends and clients became too much. They wondered why I kept such a ‘useless fixture’ in my office. Desperate to be rid of him, and unable to throw this pale, helpless man into the street, I decided on an extreme measure: I moved my entire office to a new location, leaving Bartleby behind in the empty rooms. But the story did not end there. A few days later, the new tenant of my old office came to me in a state of great excitement. Bartleby was still there. He sat on the stairs by day and slept in the entry hall by night. Everyone was disturbed. To avoid a public scandal, I went back and tried to talk to him one last time. “Bartleby," I said, “would you like to work as a store clerk?” “I would prefer not to. I am not particular,” he said. “Would you like a job traveling with someone through Europe?” “Not at all. I would prefer not to.”

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.explanation: 햇빛 아래서도 촛불 아래서도 베꼈다는 것은 "밤낮없이 열심히" 일했다는 뜻이다.

cards.badge: Bartleby was taken to the Tombs.
cards.question: the Tombs는 무엇일까?
cards.passage:
I gave up. The new tenants eventually called the police, and Bartleby was taken to the Tombs as a homeless person. When I visited him in prison, he was standing alone in a quiet courtyard, staring at a high wall. “I know where I am,” he said to me, refusing to look at me. “I have nothing to say to you.” I spoke to the prison cook, paying him to ensure Bartleby had good food. But when the cook offered him dinner, Bartleby turned his face toward the wall and said, "I prefer not to eat today." He had decided to stop eating. A few days later, I found him lying in the yard, his head resting against the stones, his eyes open but vacant. He was dead. Some months later, I heard a rumor that before coming to me, Bartleby had been a subordinate clerk in the Dead Letter Office at Washington. He had spent years sorting letters that were sent to people who were already dead, or letters that contained rings and money that would never reach their destination. These letters, intended for life, were destined for the flames. When I heard this, I could finally understand his silence and his ‘dead-wall reveries.’ Surrounded by the failed hopes and dead messages of humanity, his soul had simply given up. He had seen too much of the end of things. Ah, Bartleby! Ah, humanity!

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.explanation: the Tombs는 뉴욕 감옥의 별명이다. 바틀비는 노숙자로 그곳에 끌려갔다.

cards.badge: tales such as that of Zeuxis and Parrhasios
cards.question: 여기서 that이 가리키는 것은?
cards.passage:
The ancient Greeks felt that the visual artist’s goal was to copy visual experience. This approach appears in the realism of ancient Greek sculpture and pottery. We must sadly note that, due to the action of time and weather, no paintings from ancient Greek artists exist today. We can only surmise their quality based on tales such as that of Zeuxis and Parhassios, the obvious skill in ancient Greek sculpture, and in drawings that survive on ancient Greek pottery. This definition of art as copying reality has a problem, though. Jackson Pollock, a leader in the New York School of the 1950’s, intentionally did not copy existing objects in his art. While painting these works, Pollock and his fellow artists would consciously avoid making marks or passages that resembled recognizable objects. They succeeded at making artwork that did not copy anything, thus demonstrating that the ancient Greek view of art as mimesis ― simple copying ― does not sufficiently define art.

cards.passage:
To harness the full potential of units of measurement, we need some degree of consistency. Subjective measures contain useful knowledge, but this can be difficult to share, based as it is on an individual’s experience. The historian of science Theodore M. Porter describes measurement as a ʻtechnology of distance’: a tool that uses shared rules to bridge differences of culture and geography, allowing for the exchange of information. Following this logic, if measurement is another sort of language, then just as with words, individual units need reliable definitions in order to communicate. In the earliest societies, these definitions might need to be shared no more widely than a single settlement, meaning that the definition can be no more complex than knowing that a unit was equal to a certain body part. As these communities grew in size, though, the inadequacies of this system would become evident. Imagine a disagreement over trade or tribute: it is a moment of conflict that demands greater consistency in measurement.

In the earliest societies, these definitions might need to be shared no more widely than a single settlement, meaning that the definition can be no more complex than knowing that a unit was equal to a certain body part. As these communities grew in size, though, the inadequacies of this system would become evident. Imagine a disagreement over trade or tribute: it is a moment of conflict that demands greater consistency in measurement.

cards.badge: Even though it was old, the pillar still stood.
cards.question: Even though의 뜻은?
cards.passage:
Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Türkiye, is one of the oldest man-made structures on Earth. Experts believe it was built about 12,000 years ago. The structure consists of dozens of stone pillars arranged in rings. Many pillars are covered with carvings of animals. The tallest pillars are 5.5 meters in height and weigh more than 14,500 kilograms. At the time that Göbekli Tepe was built, there was no writing system, and people did not use metal. Even wheels did not exist. Amazingly, though, the builders were able to cut, shape, and transport 16-ton stones. Archaeologists found Stone Age tools such as knives at the site. They think hundreds of workers carved and put the pillars in place. Archaeologists are still debating the purpose of Göbekli Tepe. Klaus Schmidt ― the archaeologist who originally excavated the site ― believed that Göbekli Tepe was a holy meeting place. According to his theory, the T-shaped pillars represent human beings. The pillars face the center of the circle and perhaps represent a religious ceremony. New evidence suggests that large feasts took place at the site. Archaeologists found thousands of small animal bones nearby, with stone containers large enough to hold more than 150 liters of liquid. They also found smaller pillars similar to Göbekli Tepe’s in areas over 200 kilometers away. It’s as though Göbekli Tepe were a cathedral and the other structures were local churches.

[연습용 문장·표현]
Even though it was old, the pillar still stood.
cards.explanation: even though는 이미 사실인 내용을 인정하면서 예상과 다른 결과를 말한다. even if는 사실 여부와 관계없이 가정 조건을 말한다. 이 문장에서는 낡았다는 사실과 여전히 서 있었다는 결과가 대조된다.

cards.badge: He left early so that he could catch the bus.
cards.question: so that의 뜻은?
cards.passage:
For hundreds of years, Machu Picchu remained hidden in the Andes Mountains of Peru. In 1911, an American explorer named Hiram Bingham introduced the ancient city to the world after local people guided him there. Today, millions of visitors travel to see its beautiful stone buildings and breathtaking mountain views. Although many facts about Machu Picchu are known, historians still debate why the city was built and why it was later abandoned. Most experts believe that Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s during the rule of the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The city was probably home to nobles, priests, and skilled workers rather than a large population. People grew crops on stone terraces that covered the mountainside. They also collected fresh water through a system of carefully planned canals and fountains. These features allowed people to live comfortably in a place that was difficult to reach. One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

[연습용 문장·표현]
He left early so that he could catch the bus.
cards.explanation: so that + 주어 + can/could = ~하기 위해서(목적). so + 형용사/부사 + that(너무 ~해서)과 구분한다.

cards.badge: It was on the third day that the first crack appeared.
cards.question: 이 문장의 구조는?
cards.passage:
At first, Bartleby did an extraordinary amount of writing. As if long famishing for something to copy, he eagerly copied my documents. He copied by sunlight and by candlelight. I would have been pleased with his hard work if he had worked cheerfully. But he wrote on silently, palely, mechanically. It was on the third day of his employment that the first crack appeared in this routine. I had a document that needed to be compared for accuracy. I called to Bartleby, asking him to step behind the screen to help me check a few lines. Without moving from his seat, Bartleby replied in a unusually gentle and firm voice: “I would prefer not to.” I sat in stunned silence. I thought my ears had deceived me. I repeated my request, but the response was exactly the same. “I would prefer not to.” I looked at him. He was perfectly calm. There was no sign of anger, impatience, or rudeness in his face. Had he seemed angry or rude, I would have fired him immediately. But his calmness fascinated and paralyzed me. I could not make myself argue with him. As days passed, the situation grew more bizarre. One morning, I asked him to go to the post office; he replied that he would prefer not to. I asked him to call the other clerks to help with a task; he preferred not to. Eventually, I discovered that he had stopped writing altogether. He would spend hours standing behind his screen, staring out the window at the dead brick wall. I tried to talk to him and persuade him. “Bartleby,” I said, “why will you not write? Why will you not do anything?” “I would prefer not to,” he replied, and nothing more.

My emotions toward him were a strange mixture. Sometimes I felt a deep, melancholy pity. I realized that Bartleby was alone in the world — a lonely soul in the middle of the busy, commercial desert of Wall Street. I discovered that he never ate a full dinner; he lived almost entirely on ginger nuts. Even more shockingly, I found out one Sunday morning that he was actually living in the office. He slept on the sofa, washed his face in a small basin, and spent his weekends in the total silence of the empty business district. However, pity soon turned to a sense of dread. His presence began to affect the atmosphere of the office. I found myself, and even Turkey and Nippers, unconsciously using the word ‘prefer’ in our daily speech. His passive resistance was like a quiet plague. I felt that my authority was slowly fading before a man who did nothing, said nothing, and wanted nothing. When I finally told him he must leave, he simply preferred not to. I offered him money; he let it lie on the table. I realized that as long as he remained in my office, he was my responsibility. But the pressure from my professional friends and clients became too much. They wondered why I kept such a ‘useless fixture’ in my office. Desperate to be rid of him, and unable to throw this pale, helpless man into the street, I decided on an extreme measure: I moved my entire office to a new location, leaving Bartleby behind in the empty rooms. But the story did not end there. A few days later, the new tenant of my old office came to me in a state of great excitement. Bartleby was still there. He sat on the stairs by day and slept in the entry hall by night. Everyone was disturbed. To avoid a public scandal, I went back and tried to talk to him one last time. “Bartleby," I said, “would you like to work as a store clerk?” “I would prefer not to. I am not particular,” he said. “Would you like a job traveling with someone through Europe?” “Not at all. I would prefer not to.”

[연습용 문장·표현]

cards.explanation: It was ~ that 사이에 강조할 말(on the third day)을 넣은 강조 구문이다. 바로 사흘째 되는 날에 처음 금이 갔다.

cards.question: ‘Made of carved stone, the temple still stands.’를 Because로 시작하는 부사절 문장으로 바꾸시오.
cards.passage:
Chichén Itzá was a major city of the Maya Empire from A.D. 750 to 1200. Made of stepped pyramids, temples, and other stone structures, the ancient city is now one of Mexico’s most visited tourist destinations. The largest building in Chichén Itzá is the Temple of Kukulkan ―a pyramid with 365 steps. A kind of calendar, the temple shows the change of seasons. On the spring and autumn equinoxes each year, a shadow falls on the pyramid in the shape of a snake. As the sun sets, this shadowy snake goes down the steps to eventually join a carved snake head on the pyramid’s side. The Mayans constructed the pyramids with carved stone. Amazingly, they worked without wheels or metal tools. To build a pyramid, Mayan workers created a base and added smaller and smaller levels as the structure rose. Building the pyramids required many workers. Some pyramids took hundreds of years to complete. Chichén Itzá was both an advanced city center and a religious site. Spanish records show that the Mayans made human sacrifices to a rain god here. Archaeologists have found bones, jewelry, and other objects that people wore when they were sacrificed. Experts also know that the Mayans were knowledgeable astronomers. They used the tops of the pyramids to view Venus and other planets.

[연습용 문장·표현]
‘Made of carved stone, the temple still stands.’를 Because로 시작하는 부사절 문장으로 바꾸시오.
cards.answer: Because it is made of carved stone, the temple still stands.
criteria: Because + 주어 it + be동사 is 복원
주절 the temple still stands 유지

cards.question: ‘그 구조물은 수십 개의 돌기둥으로 구성되어 있다.’를 consist of로 한 번, be composed of로 한 번 영작하시오.
cards.passage:
Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Türkiye, is one of the oldest man-made structures on Earth. Experts believe it was built about 12,000 years ago. The structure consists of dozens of stone pillars arranged in rings. Many pillars are covered with carvings of animals. The tallest pillars are 5.5 meters in height and weigh more than 14,500 kilograms. At the time that Göbekli Tepe was built, there was no writing system, and people did not use metal. Even wheels did not exist. Amazingly, though, the builders were able to cut, shape, and transport 16-ton stones. Archaeologists found Stone Age tools such as knives at the site. They think hundreds of workers carved and put the pillars in place. Archaeologists are still debating the purpose of Göbekli Tepe. Klaus Schmidt ― the archaeologist who originally excavated the site ― believed that Göbekli Tepe was a holy meeting place. According to his theory, the T-shaped pillars represent human beings. The pillars face the center of the circle and perhaps represent a religious ceremony. New evidence suggests that large feasts took place at the site. Archaeologists found thousands of small animal bones nearby, with stone containers large enough to hold more than 150 liters of liquid. They also found smaller pillars similar to Göbekli Tepe’s in areas over 200 kilometers away. It’s as though Göbekli Tepe were a cathedral and the other structures were local churches.

[연습용 문장·표현]
‘그 구조물은 수십 개의 돌기둥으로 구성되어 있다.’를 consist of로 한 번, be composed of로 한 번 영작하시오.

cards.question: allow와 make를 각각 사용해 ‘그 도구는 그들이 돌을 옮기게 했다.’를 과거시제로 두 문장 쓰시오.
cards.passage:
For hundreds of years, Machu Picchu remained hidden in the Andes Mountains of Peru. In 1911, an American explorer named Hiram Bingham introduced the ancient city to the world after local people guided him there. Today, millions of visitors travel to see its beautiful stone buildings and breathtaking mountain views. Although many facts about Machu Picchu are known, historians still debate why the city was built and why it was later abandoned. Most experts believe that Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s during the rule of the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The city was probably home to nobles, priests, and skilled workers rather than a large population. People grew crops on stone terraces that covered the mountainside. They also collected fresh water through a system of carefully planned canals and fountains. These features allowed people to live comfortably in a place that was difficult to reach. One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

[연습용 문장·표현]
allow와 make를 각각 사용해 ‘그 도구는 그들이 돌을 옮기게 했다.’를 과거시제로 두 문장 쓰시오.

cards.question: ‘He did not work cheerfully, so I was not pleased.’를 같은 뜻의 가정법 과거완료 문장으로 바꾸시오.
cards.passage:
At first, Bartleby did an extraordinary amount of writing. As if long famishing for something to copy, he eagerly copied my documents. He copied by sunlight and by candlelight. I would have been pleased with his hard work if he had worked cheerfully. But he wrote on silently, palely, mechanically. It was on the third day of his employment that the first crack appeared in this routine. I had a document that needed to be compared for accuracy. I called to Bartleby, asking him to step behind the screen to help me check a few lines. Without moving from his seat, Bartleby replied in a unusually gentle and firm voice: “I would prefer not to.” I sat in stunned silence. I thought my ears had deceived me. I repeated my request, but the response was exactly the same. “I would prefer not to.” I looked at him. He was perfectly calm. There was no sign of anger, impatience, or rudeness in his face. Had he seemed angry or rude, I would have fired him immediately. But his calmness fascinated and paralyzed me. I could not make myself argue with him. As days passed, the situation grew more bizarre. One morning, I asked him to go to the post office; he replied that he would prefer not to. I asked him to call the other clerks to help with a task; he preferred not to. Eventually, I discovered that he had stopped writing altogether. He would spend hours standing behind his screen, staring out the window at the dead brick wall. I tried to talk to him and persuade him. “Bartleby,” I said, “why will you not write? Why will you not do anything?” “I would prefer not to,” he replied, and nothing more.

My emotions toward him were a strange mixture. Sometimes I felt a deep, melancholy pity. I realized that Bartleby was alone in the world — a lonely soul in the middle of the busy, commercial desert of Wall Street. I discovered that he never ate a full dinner; he lived almost entirely on ginger nuts. Even more shockingly, I found out one Sunday morning that he was actually living in the office. He slept on the sofa, washed his face in a small basin, and spent his weekends in the total silence of the empty business district. However, pity soon turned to a sense of dread. His presence began to affect the atmosphere of the office. I found myself, and even Turkey and Nippers, unconsciously using the word ‘prefer’ in our daily speech. His passive resistance was like a quiet plague. I felt that my authority was slowly fading before a man who did nothing, said nothing, and wanted nothing. When I finally told him he must leave, he simply preferred not to. I offered him money; he let it lie on the table. I realized that as long as he remained in my office, he was my responsibility. But the pressure from my professional friends and clients became too much. They wondered why I kept such a ‘useless fixture’ in my office. Desperate to be rid of him, and unable to throw this pale, helpless man into the street, I decided on an extreme measure: I moved my entire office to a new location, leaving Bartleby behind in the empty rooms. But the story did not end there. A few days later, the new tenant of my old office came to me in a state of great excitement. Bartleby was still there. He sat on the stairs by day and slept in the entry hall by night. Everyone was disturbed. To avoid a public scandal, I went back and tried to talk to him one last time. “Bartleby," I said, “would you like to work as a store clerk?” “I would prefer not to. I am not particular,” he said. “Would you like a job traveling with someone through Europe?” “Not at all. I would prefer not to.”

[연습용 문장·표현]
‘He did not work cheerfully, so I was not pleased.’를 같은 뜻의 가정법 과거완료 문장으로 바꾸시오.
cards.answer: If he had worked cheerfully, I would have been pleased.

cards.question: ‘Following this logic, units need reliable definitions.’를 If로 시작하는 부사절 문장으로 바꾸고, 이 문장의 동사가 과거형으로 바뀌지 않는 이유를 쓰시오.
cards.passage:
To harness the full potential of units of measurement, we need some degree of consistency. Subjective measures contain useful knowledge, but this can be difficult to share, based as it is on an individual’s experience. The historian of science Theodore M. Porter describes measurement as a ʻtechnology of distance’: a tool that uses shared rules to bridge differences of culture and geography, allowing for the exchange of information. Following this logic, if measurement is another sort of language, then just as with words, individual units need reliable definitions in order to communicate. In the earliest societies, these definitions might need to be shared no more widely than a single settlement, meaning that the definition can be no more complex than knowing that a unit was equal to a certain body part. As these communities grew in size, though, the inadequacies of this system would become evident. Imagine a disagreement over trade or tribute: it is a moment of conflict that demands greater consistency in measurement.

cards.question:
Made of stepped pyramids, the city is famous.

Made of ~ 부분의 문법 이름은? (답을 하나만 쓰세요.)
cards.passage:
Chichén Itzá was a major city of the Maya Empire from A.D. 750 to 1200. Made of stepped pyramids, temples, and other stone structures, the ancient city is now one of Mexico’s most visited tourist destinations. The largest building in Chichén Itzá is the Temple of Kukulkan ―a pyramid with 365 steps. A kind of calendar, the temple shows the change of seasons. On the spring and autumn equinoxes each year, a shadow falls on the pyramid in the shape of a snake. As the sun sets, this shadowy snake goes down the steps to eventually join a carved snake head on the pyramid’s side. The Mayans constructed the pyramids with carved stone. Amazingly, they worked without wheels or metal tools. To build a pyramid, Mayan workers created a base and added smaller and smaller levels as the structure rose. Building the pyramids required many workers. Some pyramids took hundreds of years to complete. Chichén Itzá was both an advanced city center and a religious site. Spanish records show that the Mayans made human sacrifices to a rain god here. Archaeologists have found bones, jewelry, and other objects that people wore when they were sacrificed. Experts also know that the Mayans were knowledgeable astronomers. They used the tops of the pyramids to view Venus and other planets.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.question:
one of the oldest man-made structures

man-made structures의 뜻은? (답을 하나만 쓰세요.)
cards.passage:
Göbekli Tepe, in southeastern Türkiye, is one of the oldest man-made structures on Earth. Experts believe it was built about 12,000 years ago. The structure consists of dozens of stone pillars arranged in rings. Many pillars are covered with carvings of animals. The tallest pillars are 5.5 meters in height and weigh more than 14,500 kilograms. At the time that Göbekli Tepe was built, there was no writing system, and people did not use metal. Even wheels did not exist. Amazingly, though, the builders were able to cut, shape, and transport 16-ton stones. Archaeologists found Stone Age tools such as knives at the site. They think hundreds of workers carved and put the pillars in place. Archaeologists are still debating the purpose of Göbekli Tepe. Klaus Schmidt ― the archaeologist who originally excavated the site ― believed that Göbekli Tepe was a holy meeting place. According to his theory, the T-shaped pillars represent human beings. The pillars face the center of the circle and perhaps represent a religious ceremony. New evidence suggests that large feasts took place at the site. Archaeologists found thousands of small animal bones nearby, with stone containers large enough to hold more than 150 liters of liquid. They also found smaller pillars similar to Göbekli Tepe’s in areas over 200 kilometers away. It’s as though Göbekli Tepe were a cathedral and the other structures were local churches.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
one of the oldest man-made structures

cards.passage:
For hundreds of years, Machu Picchu remained hidden in the Andes Mountains of Peru. In 1911, an American explorer named Hiram Bingham introduced the ancient city to the world after local people guided him there. Today, millions of visitors travel to see its beautiful stone buildings and breathtaking mountain views. Although many facts about Machu Picchu are known, historians still debate why the city was built and why it was later abandoned. Most experts believe that Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s during the rule of the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The city was probably home to nobles, priests, and skilled workers rather than a large population. People grew crops on stone terraces that covered the mountainside. They also collected fresh water through a system of carefully planned canals and fountains. These features allowed people to live comfortably in a place that was difficult to reach. One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

I am an elderly man. For the past thirty years, my work as a lawyer has brought me into contact with a particular class of men: the law-copyists, or scriveners. I have known many of them, and could tell many stories that might make you smile or weep. But I’ll leave out the biographies of all other scriveners for a few passages from the life of Bartleby, who was the strangest I ever saw or heard of. At the time of this story, my office was located on Wall Street. On one side, my windows looked out upon the white wall of the interior of a spacious sky-light shaft. On the other side, my windows commanded an unobstructed view of a lofty brick wall, black by age and everlasting shade. This view was not exactly beautiful, but it was at least quiet. I already had two scriveners: Turkey and Nippers. Turkey was a short, fat Englishman who worked wonderfully in the morning, but after his lunch, his face would turn red, and he became energetic but reckless and messy with his ink. Nippers, on the other hand, was a victim of ambition and indigestion. He was nervous and irritable in the morning, but calm and productive in the afternoon. Between them, I had a functional office, provided it was the right time of day. There was also Ginger Nut, my twelve-year-old errand boy, whose most important duty was to buy apples and ginger nuts for the scriveners. But as my business grew, I needed more help. In answer to my advertisement, a young man appeared on my office threshold one morning. He was pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, and incurably forlorn. He was Bartleby. After a brief interview, I hired him. I gave him a seat at a desk near my own, separated by a high green screen. I wanted him to be close enough for me to hand him papers, but private enough to keep his quiet nature intact.

cards.question:
Bartleby was taken to the Tombs.

the Tombs는 무엇일까? (답을 하나만 쓰세요.)
cards.passage:
I gave up. The new tenants eventually called the police, and Bartleby was taken to the Tombs as a homeless person. When I visited him in prison, he was standing alone in a quiet courtyard, staring at a high wall. “I know where I am,” he said to me, refusing to look at me. “I have nothing to say to you.” I spoke to the prison cook, paying him to ensure Bartleby had good food. But when the cook offered him dinner, Bartleby turned his face toward the wall and said, "I prefer not to eat today." He had decided to stop eating. A few days later, I found him lying in the yard, his head resting against the stones, his eyes open but vacant. He was dead. Some months later, I heard a rumor that before coming to me, Bartleby had been a subordinate clerk in the Dead Letter Office at Washington. He had spent years sorting letters that were sent to people who were already dead, or letters that contained rings and money that would never reach their destination. These letters, intended for life, were destined for the flames. When I heard this, I could finally understand his silence and his ‘dead-wall reveries.’ Surrounded by the failed hopes and dead messages of humanity, his soul had simply given up. He had seen too much of the end of things. Ah, Bartleby! Ah, humanity!

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]

cards.question:
tales such as that of Zeuxis and Parrhasios

여기서 that이 가리키는 것은? (답을 하나만 쓰세요.)
cards.passage:
The ancient Greeks felt that the visual artist’s goal was to copy visual experience. This approach appears in the realism of ancient Greek sculpture and pottery. We must sadly note that, due to the action of time and weather, no paintings from ancient Greek artists exist today. We can only surmise their quality based on tales such as that of Zeuxis and Parhassios, the obvious skill in ancient Greek sculpture, and in drawings that survive on ancient Greek pottery. This definition of art as copying reality has a problem, though. Jackson Pollock, a leader in the New York School of the 1950’s, intentionally did not copy existing objects in his art. While painting these works, Pollock and his fellow artists would consciously avoid making marks or passages that resembled recognizable objects. They succeeded at making artwork that did not copy anything, thus demonstrating that the ancient Greek view of art as mimesis ― simple copying ― does not sufficiently define art.

One of the most impressive features of Machu Picchu is its stonework. The Inca builders shaped huge stones so carefully that they fit together without mortar. This method made the buildings strong enough to survive many earthquakes. Even after hundreds of years of wind, rain, and earthquakes, much of the city still stands. Machu Picchu shows that the Inca people were not only skilled builders but also talented engineers who understood both nature and architecture.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
These features allowed people ____ comfortably.
cards.answer: to live. allow + 목적어 + to V는 "~가 …하게 해 주다"다. 목적격 보어 자리에 to부정사가 온다.
criteria: 근거: allow + 목적어 + to V는 "~가 …하게 해 주다"다. 목적격 보어 자리에 to부정사가 온다.

cards.question:
They built it without wheels or metal tools.

without wheels or metal tools의 뜻은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.

[연습용 문장·표현]
They built it without wheels or metal tools.
cards.answer: 바퀴도 금속 도구도 없이. without A or B = A도 B도 없이. 마야인과 괴베클리 테페의 건설자들은 바퀴도 금속 도구도 없이 거대한 돌을 다뤘다.
criteria: 근거: without A or B = A도 B도 없이. 마야인과 괴베클리 테페의 건설자들은 바퀴도 금속 도구도 없이 거대한 돌을 다뤘다.

cards.question:
a person who copied legal documents by hand

이런 일을 한 사람을 뜻하는 말은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.passage:
I am an elderly man. For the past thirty years, my work as a lawyer has brought me into contact with a particular class of men: the law-copyists, or scriveners. I have known many of them, and could tell many stories that might make you smile or weep. But I’ll leave out the biographies of all other scriveners for a few passages from the life of Bartleby, who was the strangest I ever saw or heard of. At the time of this story, my office was located on Wall Street. On one side, my windows looked out upon the white wall of the interior of a spacious sky-light shaft. On the other side, my windows commanded an unobstructed view of a lofty brick wall, black by age and everlasting shade. This view was not exactly beautiful, but it was at least quiet. I already had two scriveners: Turkey and Nippers. Turkey was a short, fat Englishman who worked wonderfully in the morning, but after his lunch, his face would turn red, and he became energetic but reckless and messy with his ink. Nippers, on the other hand, was a victim of ambition and indigestion. He was nervous and irritable in the morning, but calm and productive in the afternoon. Between them, I had a functional office, provided it was the right time of day. There was also Ginger Nut, my twelve-year-old errand boy, whose most important duty was to buy apples and ginger nuts for the scriveners. But as my business grew, I needed more help. In answer to my advertisement, a young man appeared on my office threshold one morning. He was pallidly neat, pitiably respectable, and incurably forlorn. He was Bartleby. After a brief interview, I hired him. I gave him a seat at a desk near my own, separated by a high green screen. I wanted him to be close enough for me to hand him papers, but private enough to keep his quiet nature intact.

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
a person who copied legal documents by hand
cards.answer: scrivener (필경사). scrivener(필경사)는 법률 문서와 계약서를 손으로 베껴 쓰던 사람이다. 기계 부품처럼 대체 가능한 존재로 취급됐다.
criteria: 근거: scrivener(필경사)는 법률 문서와 계약서를 손으로 베껴 쓰던 사람이다. 기계 부품처럼 대체 가능한 존재로 취급됐다.

cards.question:
As if famishing for something to copy, he copied eagerly.

As if의 뜻은? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.passage:
At first, Bartleby did an extraordinary amount of writing. As if long famishing for something to copy, he eagerly copied my documents. He copied by sunlight and by candlelight. I would have been pleased with his hard work if he had worked cheerfully. But he wrote on silently, palely, mechanically. It was on the third day of his employment that the first crack appeared in this routine. I had a document that needed to be compared for accuracy. I called to Bartleby, asking him to step behind the screen to help me check a few lines. Without moving from his seat, Bartleby replied in a unusually gentle and firm voice: “I would prefer not to.” I sat in stunned silence. I thought my ears had deceived me. I repeated my request, but the response was exactly the same. “I would prefer not to.” I looked at him. He was perfectly calm. There was no sign of anger, impatience, or rudeness in his face. Had he seemed angry or rude, I would have fired him immediately. But his calmness fascinated and paralyzed me. I could not make myself argue with him. As days passed, the situation grew more bizarre. One morning, I asked him to go to the post office; he replied that he would prefer not to. I asked him to call the other clerks to help with a task; he preferred not to. Eventually, I discovered that he had stopped writing altogether. He would spend hours standing behind his screen, staring out the window at the dead brick wall. I tried to talk to him and persuade him. “Bartleby,” I said, “why will you not write? Why will you not do anything?” “I would prefer not to,” he replied, and nothing more.

My emotions toward him were a strange mixture. Sometimes I felt a deep, melancholy pity. I realized that Bartleby was alone in the world — a lonely soul in the middle of the busy, commercial desert of Wall Street. I discovered that he never ate a full dinner; he lived almost entirely on ginger nuts. Even more shockingly, I found out one Sunday morning that he was actually living in the office. He slept on the sofa, washed his face in a small basin, and spent his weekends in the total silence of the empty business district. However, pity soon turned to a sense of dread. His presence began to affect the atmosphere of the office. I found myself, and even Turkey and Nippers, unconsciously using the word ‘prefer’ in our daily speech. His passive resistance was like a quiet plague. I felt that my authority was slowly fading before a man who did nothing, said nothing, and wanted nothing. When I finally told him he must leave, he simply preferred not to. I offered him money; he let it lie on the table. I realized that as long as he remained in my office, he was my responsibility. But the pressure from my professional friends and clients became too much. They wondered why I kept such a ‘useless fixture’ in my office. Desperate to be rid of him, and unable to throw this pale, helpless man into the street, I decided on an extreme measure: I moved my entire office to a new location, leaving Bartleby behind in the empty rooms. But the story did not end there. A few days later, the new tenant of my old office came to me in a state of great excitement. Bartleby was still there. He sat on the stairs by day and slept in the entry hall by night. Everyone was disturbed. To avoid a public scandal, I went back and tried to talk to him one last time. “Bartleby," I said, “would you like to work as a store clerk?” “I would prefer not to. I am not particular,” he said. “Would you like a job traveling with someone through Europe?” “Not at all. I would prefer not to.”

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
As if famishing for something to copy, he copied eagerly.
cards.answer: 마치 ~인 것처럼. as if = as though(마치 ~인 것처럼). famishing은 "몹시 굶주린"이다.
criteria: 근거: as if = as though(마치 ~인 것처럼). famishing은 "몹시 굶주린"이다.

cards.question:
Bartleby was taken to the Tombs.

the Tombs는 무엇일까? 답과 그 이유를 연결하여 서술하시오.
cards.passage:
I gave up. The new tenants eventually called the police, and Bartleby was taken to the Tombs as a homeless person. When I visited him in prison, he was standing alone in a quiet courtyard, staring at a high wall. “I know where I am,” he said to me, refusing to look at me. “I have nothing to say to you.” I spoke to the prison cook, paying him to ensure Bartleby had good food. But when the cook offered him dinner, Bartleby turned his face toward the wall and said, "I prefer not to eat today." He had decided to stop eating. A few days later, I found him lying in the yard, his head resting against the stones, his eyes open but vacant. He was dead. Some months later, I heard a rumor that before coming to me, Bartleby had been a subordinate clerk in the Dead Letter Office at Washington. He had spent years sorting letters that were sent to people who were already dead, or letters that contained rings and money that would never reach their destination. These letters, intended for life, were destined for the flames. When I heard this, I could finally understand his silence and his ‘dead-wall reveries.’ Surrounded by the failed hopes and dead messages of humanity, his soul had simply given up. He had seen too much of the end of things. Ah, Bartleby! Ah, humanity!

[문제의 대상 문장·표현]
Bartleby was taken to the Tombs.
cards.answer: 뉴욕 감옥의 별명. the Tombs는 뉴욕 감옥의 별명이다. 바틀비는 노숙자로 그곳에 끌려갔다.
criteria: 근거: the Tombs는 뉴욕 감옥의 별명이다. 바틀비는 노숙자로 그곳에 끌려갔다.
